processing: Japanese steamed green tea, made in the usual way of steaming, rolling and drying; the character comes mainly from high, misty gardens.
harvest_season: Spring first flush is the most valued, as with Japanese green tea generally.
appearance_dry: Dark green needles, typical of Japanese steamed green tea.
taste_profile: Mellow and low in astringency, the reason it has a name among Gifu teas.

brewing.notes: Its appeal is softness, so keep the water cool in the first steep and do not overleaf.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's tea, spring first flush at the top. It is a tea to drink fresh, within the year, with no ageing tradition behind it.
description:
Shirakawa-cha comes from the hills of Shirakawa town and Higashishirakawa village in Kamo District, Gifu. It is one of the two main brands of Gifu tea and the more upland one, with gardens on the slopes along the Shirakawa, Kurokawa and Akagawa rivers.

The height is the point. Fields lie at up to about 600 to 700 metres, river mist hangs in the mornings and evenings, and the soil is red clay. The making itself follows the normal steamed green tea route.

The cup is known for mildness: little astringency and a rounded feel, with much of the production aimed at the better grades. Cool water plays to that strength.

You may read that this is Japan's northern limit for tea. It is not: Toyama and Niigata also grow tea. Buy it for the mellow mountain cup, and look for the Mino-Shirakawa name, which is tied by label rules to the local distribution area.
history:
The usual account places the start around 1400, in the Muromachi period, when the priest of Banryu-ji temple in Osawa, now part of Higashishirakawa, brought seedlings from Uji and encouraged villagers to grow them. The temple itself was closed in the anti-Buddhist measures of the early Meiji years.

Proper production dates from the early Edo period, the 1600s. Around 1970, tea served to passengers at Shirakawaguchi station on the Takayama Line is said to have made the name known nationally.
